Effect of air mixing on high-solids anaerobic digestion of cow manure: 
Performance and mechanism 
Xinwei Li a, Liangwei Deng b,c, Fucheng Li a,c, Dan Zheng b,c, Hongnan Yang b,c,* 
a Department of Environment and Resources, Southwest University of Science and Technology, Mianyang 621010, PR China 
b Biogas Institute of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China 
c Key Laboratory of Development and Application of Rural Renewable Energy, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Effect of air mixing on high-solids 
anaerobic digestion of cow manure was 
studied. 
• Optimal air mixing intensity of 37.5 
mL/(L⋅min) enhanced CH4 production 
by 13 %. 
• Air mixing improved the hydrolysis of 
macromolecular substrate and carbon 
recovery. 
• Air mixing enriched SOB, SAOB and 
aceticlastic methanogen. 
• Predicted hydrolase demonstrated high 
abundance under air mixing condition.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Biogas production 
Waste management 
Gas mixing 
Microbial community 
Hydrolysis 
A B S T R A C T   
This study aimed to further investigate the effect of air mixing on the performance of a high-solids anaerobic 
digestion system and reveal its underlying mechanisms via analyses of carbon conversion, microbial commu­
nities and key functional genes. When the air mixing intensity was 12.5, 37.5 and 62.5 mL/(L‧min), compared 
with the anaerobic digestion without air mixing, the methane yield was increased by 6 %, 13 % and 6 %, 
respectively. The improved performance was partly attributed to the increased hydrolysis rate of macromolecular 
substances by 5 %–16 % and carbon recovery in the form of methane by 6 %–7% compared with the controls. 
Functional flora (Magnetospirillum, Synergistaceae) and hydrolytic metabolism-related enzymes (cellulose, 
α-amylase) demonstrated higher abundance under air mixing condition, thus promoting the degradation of 
organic matter and methane production. This work provides some new insights into the use of air mixing to 
improve anaerobic digestion of high-solids waste.   
1. Introduction 
Mixing is an essential part of anaerobic digestion (AD) process and 
proper mixing can promote mass and heat transfer, improve degradation 
and transformation efficiency of organic matter and biogas escape 
(Lindmark et al., 2014). The main AD mixing modes include biogas

mixing, mechanical mixing and hydraulic mixing (Yang et al., 2021). 
With regard to long-term operation, biogas mixing is preferred over 
other mixing methods due to lower energy demand, lower operation cost 
and higher operation reliability (Dapelo et al., 2015; Yang & Deng, 
2020). However, biogas mixing can be affected by its own biogas pro­
duction, and full mixing cannot be achieved when biogas production is 
insufficient, which restricts its application in on-farm biogas plants 
(Yang & Deng, 2020). 
In order to solve the problems of insufficient biogas production 
associated with biogas mixing, Yang & Deng (2020) combined with the 
latest research progress on the tolerance mechanism of AD system to 
trace oxygen (this process is generally referred to as “micro-aeration”) 
(Fu et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2022b) put forward a new 
mixing method, air mixing. Compared with micro-aeration, air mixing 
can improve mass transfer and create a micro-oxygen environment. Air 
mixing led to an increase both in methane (CH4) yield by 6 %–20 % and 
in hydrogen sulfide (H2S) removal rate from biogas by 63 %–70 % 
compared to the other mixing modes (Yang & Deng, 2020). The mass 
transfer and micro-oxygen environment established by air mixing 
contributed to increases in CH4 yield at rates of 63 % and 37 %, 
respectively (Yang & Deng, 2020). In addition, the stable operation and 
good biogas production of a full-scale continuous stirred tank reactor 
using air mixing for more than one year also verified the feasibility of air 
mixing (Yang et al., 2021). 
However, previous studies have mainly applied air mixing or micro- 
aeration to the low-solids anaerobic digestion system with a total solids 
(TS) concentration between 2.5 % and 6.0 % (Fu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 
2022a; Zeb et al., 2022). Thus, it was not possible to comprehensively 
assess the applicability of air mixing in the AD process. In addition, the 
optimal process parameters of air mixing require further study. If the air 
mixing intensity is too high, it will have a certain negative impact on 
anaerobic digestion and reduce the output of biogas (Lindmark et al., 
2014). Therefore, the purpose of this study was to investigate the effect 
of different air mixing intensities on the high-solids AD of cow manure 
by analyzing and comparing the hydrolysis efficiency and CH4 
production. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Substrate and inoculum 
Fresh cow manure was collected from a beef cattle farm located in 
Jianyang, China and used as the substrate in this experiment. The cow 
manure was stored in a refrigerator at 4℃ before use. The TS concen­
tration and volatile solids (VS) concentration of cow manure were 21.8 
% and 16.6 %, respectively. The sludge collected from a biogas plant 
treating animal wastewater was used as inoculum, with TS and VS 
concentrations of 10.2 % and 5.0 %, respectively (see Supporting 
Information). 
2.2. Experimental design 
To conduct the AD batch experiments, 8 glass bottles (each 1.0 L with 
a working volume of 0.8 L) were used (see Supporting Information). An 
aeration head was included in the glass bottle for air intake. All glass 
bottles were inserted into a thermostatic water bath at 35 ± 1 ◦C. Before 
AD, 75 g (wet weight) cow manure and 600 g (wet weight) inoculum 
were mixed in glass bottles. The amount ratio of inoculum to substrate 
(both expressed in g of VS) was 2:1 and the final TS concentration of the 
AD system was approximately 10 %. Biogas production with inoculum 
only (i.e., no cow manure) was also carried out as the blank group. 
Four treatments were conducted with air mixing intensity of 0 (i.e., 
control), 12.5, 37.5 and 62.5 mL/(L‧min), and were referred to as R-ck, 
R-12.5, R-37.5 and R-62.5, respectively, with two in parallel in each 
group. Air was manually injected into the bottles using a syringe once a 
day for 1 min each time. 
2.3. Analysis method 
The daily biogas production was measured with a gas flowmeter 
(Ritter, Germany), and the amount of injected air for mixing was 
deducted from daily biogas production. The methods used to determine 
TS, VS biogas composition, crude fiber and crude fat were according to a 
previous study (Yang & Deng, 2020). 
The analysis of mass balance was performed to determine the carbon 
(C) recovery after AD of cow manure under different air mixing in­
tensities. For carbon mass balance analysis, the mixed samples before 
AD (cow manure and sludge) and after AD (digestate and sludge) were 
collected from the treatment groups and control group. The carbon 
content (gC) in mixed samples was determined using a total organic 
carbon (TOC) analyzer (TOC-VCPH, Shimadzu). CH4 and CO2 data from 
biogas production at normal temperature and pressure (273oK and 1 
atm) were converted to gC using the ideal gas law equation. The con­
version details can be found in a previous study (Nguyen et al., 2019). 
The carbon mass balance in the treatment groups and control group was 
analyzed based on the principle of mass conservation. 
2.4. Analysis of microorganisms 
In order to avoid interference due to residual DNA from dead cells in 
the AD system on microbial analysis, RNA extracted from sludge samples 
was selected for high-throughput sequencing in this study. The sludge 
sample was collected in a centrifuge tube at the end of the experiment. 
RNA was rapidly extracted according to the E.Z.N.A.® Soil RNA Mini Kit 
(Omega Bio-Tek, USA). The purified RNA was subsequently used to 
synthesize complementary DNA (cDNA) using HiScript® Q RT SuperMix 
for the qPCR kit (Vazyme). The high-throughput sequencing of cDNA 
samples was performed on the Illumina Miseq platform (Majorbio, 
China). The raw sequence data files were deposited at NCBI GenBank 
project (PRJNA906293). The detailed method description and bioin­
formatics analysis were described in a previous study (Yang & Deng, 
2020). 
Functional prediction analysis was performed on the Majorbio Cloud 
Platform (https://www.majorbio.com/). The PICRUSt2 (Phylogenetic 
Investigation of Communities by Reconstruction of Unobserved States) 
was applied to evaluate the expression of key enzymes in hydrolytic 
metabolism based on 16S rRNA data, and the KEGG (Kyoto Encyclo­
pedia of Genes and Genomes) database was used to support functional 
gene profiling. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Biogas production performance 
Fig. 1a shows the changes in cumulative biogas production following 
AD of cow manure under different air mixing intensities. The maximum 
cumulative biogas production (Pmax) of experimental groups R-12.5, R- 
37.5 and R-62.5 was 294, 316 and 299 mL/gTS, respectively, and was 
increased by 4.3 %, 12.1 % and 6.0 % compared with the control group 
(282 mL/gTS), respectively (see Supporting Information). The 
maximum cumulative methane production (Pmax-CH4) of experimental 
groups R-12.5, R-37.5 and R-62.5 was 185, 198 and 186 CH4/gTS, 
respectively. Compared with the control group (175 mL CH4/gTS), the 
methanogenic efficiency was increased by 5.7 %, 13.1 % and 6.3 %, 
respectively (see Supporting Information). Other studies have also re­
ported that micro-aeration improved methane yield from cellulosic 
substrates (Zhan et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2022c; Fu et al., 2016). How­
ever, direct comparisons between these studies were difficult due to the 
different compositions of the substrates and operational conditions. 
The above results indicated that when the air mixing intensity was 
37.5 mL/(L‧min), the CH4 production was markedly improved. Although 
the CH4 content in this group was reduced to 53 % due to the dilution of 
injected air, it did not affect the normal use of biogas (>50 %)

(Nallamothu et al., 2013). However, when the intensity of air mixing 
was high, the efficiency of improvement decreased. This may be because 
the excess O2 was not timely consumed by facultative bacteria in the 
early stage of AD, which does not produce a strict anaerobic reducing 
environment, thus inhibiting the activity of strict anaerobic metha­
nogens. Alternatively, facultative bacteria perform aerobic respiration, 
converting organic matter to CO2 instead of CH4 (Botheju & Bakke, 
2011). 
3.2. Hydrolysis of macromolecular substances 
The hydrolysis of macromolecular substances into soluble organics is 
generally considered as the rate-limiting step during AD of feedstock 
with a high-solids concentration (Yu et al., 2021). In this study, samples 
of cow manure AD on day 0 (marked as R) and day 23 were taken to 
determine the content of crude fiber and crude fat. The results showed 
that air mixing promoted the removal efficiency of crude fiber and crude 
fat (see Fig. 1b). Compared with control group R-ck, the removal rates of 
crude fiber in experimental groups R-12.5, R-37.5 and R-62.5 were 
increased by 10 %, 11 % and 5 %, and the removal rates of crude fat 
were increased by 9 %, 13 % and 16 %, respectively. The removal rate of 
crude fiber was the highest at the air mixing intensity of 37.5 mL/(L‧ 
min), and showed a downward trend at the mixing intensity of 62.5 mL/ 
(L‧min). Zeb et al. (2022) also reached a similar conclusion where the 
lignin removal rate decreased as the micro-aeration dose increased. This 
may be due to the damaging effect of high oxygen flow on the lignin 
hydrolysis process, but the specific reasons for this require further 
investigation. 
3.3. Carbon conversion 
In the AD process, it is hoped that the carbon from feedstock can be 
converted into CH4 as much as possible by microorganisms (Tian et al., 
2022). Therefore, a carbon mass balance analysis was conducted in this 
study, and the results are shown in Fig. 1c. The carbon contents in CH4 of 
the R-ck, R-12.5, R-37.5 and R-62.5 groups accounted for 6 %, 6 %, 7 % 
and 6 % of the total carbon contents in the fermented materials, 
respectively. These results showed that the biodegradation of lignocel­
lulose and other refractory substances in cow manure was raised under 
air mixing condition, and more dissolved substrates were converted into 
biogas, which indicated that air mixing promoted carbon recovery. 
Moreover, when the air mixing intensity was 37.5 mL/(L‧min), the 
carbon recovered in the form of CH4 was the highest; when the air 
mixing intensity was 62.5 mL/(L‧min), more carbon was converted to 
CO2. 
3.4. Microbial community characterization 
The relative abundance of bacterial and archaeal communities at the 
genus level under different air mixing intensities are shown in Fig. 2a 
and 2b. Magnetospirillum is a sulfide-oxidizing bacterium (SOB) (Hao­
sagul et al., 2021). Smithella, Thiovirga, Thiokalimicrobium and Hydro­
genophaga were also reported to play important roles in sulfide oxidation 
(Haosagul et al., 2021). The total abundance of these SOBs was 5 %, 5 %, 
7 % and 11 % in R-ck, R-12.5, R-37.5 and R-62.5, respectively. Ac­
cording to the KEGG database, sulfide oxidization is likely catalyzed by 
either sulfide:quinone reductase (EC1.8.5.4) or flavocytochrome c sul­
fide dehydrogenase (EC1.8.2.3). PICRUSt-based prediction of sulfur 
metabolism-related enzymes only detected the flavocytochrome c sul­
fide dehydrogenase in this study. The predicted abundance of fla­
vocytochrome c sulfide dehydrogenase was 45 % to 195 % higher in R- 
37.5 (756) and R-62.5 (1537) than in R-ck (521). These results showed 
that air mixing increased the abundance of SOB and related enzyme 
activities, which was conducive to the removal of H2S. Synergistaceae is a 
syntrophic acetate-oxidizing bacteria (SAOB), which could oxidize 
acetic acid to CO2 and H2 as substrates for methanogenesis (Zhu et al., 
2022a). The abundance of Synergistaceae in all groups was 4 % (R-37.5) 
> 2 % (R-62.5) > 1 % (R-12.5) > 1 % (R-ck). An enrichment of SOB and 
SAOB is conducive to desulfurization, VFA degradation and 
methanogenesis. 
Methanosaeta was the dominant archaea in all experimental groups, 
with an abundance of 52 %–61 % (Fig. 2b). Compared with the control 
group (R-ck), the relative abundance of Methanosaeta in the air mixing 
groups (R-12.5, R-37.5 and R-62.5) increased by 5 %, 16 % and 8 %, 
respectively, indicating that air mixing favored the growth of Meth­
anosaeta. Previous studies on microaerobic systems also demonstrated 
that Methanosaeta was enriched at low oxygen concentrations (Guo 
et al., 2021). Methanosaeta belongs to the acetoclastic methanogens and 
dominates at low acetate concentrations (Zhou et al., 2021). The 
oxidation of acetate through aerobic respiration to maintain a dynamic

3.5. Hydrolase prediction 
The abundance of functional enzymes related to hydrolytic meta­
bolism was studied by PICRUSt2 based on 16S rRNA gene data in this 
section. Cellulose and hemicellulose are the main macromolecular 
organic matter in cow manure and account for approximately 50 % of 
the total solids (Zhao et al., 2018). Cellulase and beta-glucosidase 
(EC3.2.1.4 and EC3.2.1.21) have been reported to degrade lignocellu­
lose (Zhu et al., 2022b). Fig. 2c shows that the abundance of cellulase in 
the R-37.5 was the highest, and was 1.4 times than that in the R-ck, 
However, the abundance of cellulase in the R-62.5 was the lowest, which 
might be an important reason for the reduction in the crude fiber 
removal rate when the air mixing intensity increased to 62.5 mL/ 
(L•min) (see Section 3.2). The predicted beta-glucosidase abundance 
was 6 % to 19 % higher in the experimental groups (R-12.5, R-37.5 and 
R-62.5) than in the control group (R-ck) (Fig. 2c). Triacylglycerol lipase 
(EC3.1.1.3), phospholipase A(1) (EC3.1.1.32) and phospholipase A(2) 
(EC3.1.1.4) are important lipid hydrolases (Reihaneh et al., 2022). The 
predicted abundance of lipid hydrolases in this study was very low (see 
Supporting Information), which might be related to the lower lipid 
content in cow manure. It was observed that the relative abundance of 
lipid hydrolase in all groups was R-62.5 > R-37.5 > R-12.5 > R-ck, 
which was consistent with the change in crude fat removal rate (Fig. 1b). 
The above results proved that the relative abundance of hydrolysis- 
related extracellular enzymes in the reactor with air mixing was 
generally higher than that in the reactor without air mixing, indicating 
that air mixing stimulated the secretion of extracellular enzymes and 
accelerated the degradation of macromolecular organic matter and 
further facilitated the production of CH4. 
4. Conclusion 
The effect of air mixing on the high-solids AD of cow manure was 
successfully investigated. Air mixing increased methane production by 
6–13 %, enhanced hydrolysis of macromolecular substrates, and 
improved carbon recovery. Microbial community structure analysis 
showed that air mixing optimized microbial community structure, 
resulted in higher relative abundance of sulfide-oxidizing bacteria 
(Magnetospirillum), syntrophic acetate-oxidizing bacteria (Synergista­
ceae) and aceticlastic methanogen (Methanosaeta). Hydrolytic meta­
bolism 
related 
enzymes 
including 
cellulase, 
α-amylase, 
and 
triacylglycerol lipase predicted by PICRUSt2 based on 16S rRNA gene 
data demonstrated high abundance of hydrolase under air mixing 
conditions.
